archetype.name: Bubble Team (offense-starved)
archetype.definition: Last season's fringe playoff team, now sliding below the line: it holds the puck and gets competent goaltending, but the league's thinnest attack and a leaky penalty kill keep dragging it under .500.

report.headline: Columbus owns the puck but can't score, and last year's 92 points looks distant.
report.take:
Columbus is 9-12-0, seventh in the Metropolitan and 26th of 32 on the site. That record is not a fluke in either direction. The goal difference per game ranks 27th, and Pts vs Goal Diff sits at a near-neutral -0.6, so the standings say what the scoreboard says. The 82-game pace is 70 points. Last season this team finished with 92 points and ranked 16th on the site, so this is a real step back, not a slow start for a bad club.

The defense is not the main problem. Goals allowed run at 3.24 a game, 18th and almost exactly league average. The trouble is at the other end: the offense ranks 32nd by goals per game, and the scoring rate trails the league by 0.63. The odd part is that Columbus has the puck. Its 51% CF % ranks 8th, yet its xGF % is 48.2%, 22nd. The Blue Jackets carry possession without getting to the dangerous areas, a sharp drop from last year's 52% xGF %. Nor is this a cold-shooting story. All-situations Shooting % is 10.3%, above the league's 9.8%. The goals are missing because the chances are thin, and better luck won't supply those.

The roster helps explain it. The most-used forward, Cole Sillinger, plays 15.92 minutes a night and has 9 points, and the forward group grades C-. The goaltending (C+) has been roughly average overall, but that average hides a split. Cam Talbot is at .907 with a 5.5 GSAx, while Jet Greaves is at .875 and -3.4, and the starts have been close to even. One more quirk: opposing defensemen collect 47.8% of the points scored against Columbus, against a league norm of 29.3%. The Blue Jackets hold opposing forwards well under their usual output, but point shots and activated defensemen keep hurting them, probably on a penalty kill that is killing only 72.4%.

The direction is flat rather than collapsing. November scoring rose to 2.78 a game from 2.42 in October, and the last 10 games ran almost exactly at season form. There's a decent possession team in here, but without more shot quality and a functional kill, this looks like a mid-70s-point team rather than last year's 90s.

strengths.title: Talbot is holding up his end
strengths.body: Cam Talbot's .907 Save % and 5.5 GSAx put him 16th of 72 on the goalie tab, and he is the reason team GSAx is positive at 2 (12th). The defense is average largely because he steals a few. A veteran with real GSAx over 11 starts is a reasonable bet to stay solid, but not to carry the team alone.

strengths.title: Possession is real
strengths.body: A 51% CF % ranks 8th, in line with last season's 51%, so the puck-carrying identity has survived the slide. That is the structural base a better team is built on. It is also what makes the poor results feel fixable, provided the attempts start coming from better spots.

strengths.title: Opposing forwards get shut down
strengths.body: Against Columbus, opposing forwards produce well under their own averages, the 4th-best mark in the league, and wingers are held to the same rank. The checking structure in the middle of the ice works, and with a full season of it behind them, that is likely to hold.

concerns.title: Last in the league at scoring
concerns.body: The offense ranks 32nd by goals per game, and the gap to the league is 0.63 goals a night. With xGF % at 48.2% despite good possession, the shortfall is in chance quality, not finishing luck: shooting is above league average. That kind of problem rarely fixes itself without personnel or system changes.

concerns.title: Penalty kill bleeding goals
concerns.body: PK % is 72.4%, 25th and well below the league's 77.2%. It is also worse than last season's 76%, and it fits the unusual share of points going to opposing defensemen. Kills tend to drift back toward average, but this one has room to fall before it does.

concerns.title: The Greaves starts are costly
concerns.body: Jet Greaves has started 10 games with a .875 Save % and -3.4 GSAx, 54th of 72 on the tab. The tandem has been close to a coin flip on starts. If that continues, the advantage Talbot builds keeps leaking away.

trend.note: Columbus went 5-7 in October and 4-5 in November, with scoring up a bit and goals against flat at about 3.2 a game. A five-game losing streak in mid-November was offset by the two road wins that closed the last 10, and the recent stretch matches the season almost exactly.

weekAhead.headline: Two cracks at shaky Devils goaltending, then Detroit and Pittsburgh
weekAhead.body:
The week opens with a home-and-home against New Jersey (15-8-0). The Devils are the better team on paper: 4th in offense, 4th in xGF %, 2nd in CF %. They also allow the 2nd-fewest shots, which is bad news for an offense already struggling to create. Their weakness is the net and the kill. Devils goaltending grades D with a -9.4 GSAx, and their 64.2% PK % ranks 30th. Columbus will be outshot in these two games; to win them, it needs to convert on the power play and get Talbot in goal.

The back half is softer. Detroit (8-12-3, 25th on the site) scores even less than Columbus at an offRank of 30, and its 6% Shooting % is 25th. Pittsburgh (7-14-2, 28th) sits below the Blue Jackets in the division, with an F-graded blueline and a defense that lets centers score well above their averages. Two wins in those games would make it a decent week; a split of the four games overall is the most likely result.

keyMatchups.title: Columbus power play vs. Devils kill
keyMatchups.body: New Jersey kills only 64.2% of penalties, 30th in the league, and its goalies sit 29th in GSAx. Columbus's 20.4% power play is below average, but this is the best special-teams matchup it will see. Goals here count double for a team that struggles to score at 5-on-5.

keyMatchups.title: Devils possession vs. Columbus possession
keyMatchups.body: Columbus's 51% CF % has been its calling card, but New Jersey's 56% ranks 2nd and its xGF % is 55.5%. Expect the Blue Jackets to spend more time defending than usual. That raises the stakes on the goalie choice for both games.

keyMatchups.title: Centers against a soft Penguins defense
keyMatchups.body: Pittsburgh ranks 31st at holding centers to their averages, and its blueline grades F. Sillinger, the most-used forward, should find room on Nov. 30. Beware, though: the Penguins' 82% PK % ranks 9th, so Columbus will need to win that game at even strength.

weekAhead.watch: Who starts in goal against New Jersey: Talbot (.907, +5.5 GSAx) gives Columbus a chance to survive the Devils' territorial edge, while Greaves (.875) probably does not.

restOfSeason.body:
The underlying numbers point to roughly the team the record shows: a bit better at possession than last season's version, clearly worse at creating quality chances, with average goaltending and a weak penalty kill. Some of the gap should close. The PK should drift up toward league norms, and November's scoring improvement over October is a small sign the offense isn't stuck at the bottom. Nothing here looks inflated, so there is no collapse waiting either. PDO and Pts vs Goal Diff are both near neutral.

What isn't coming back without changes is last season's 52% xGF %. A team that converts possession into chances at this rate tends to finish below .500. My range is 33 to 38 wins and 72 to 82 standings points, short of last season's 92 and outside the playoff picture in a Metropolitan where Carolina and New Jersey are already well clear.
swingFactors: Talbot taking a clear majority of starts
Turning possession into quality chances (xGF % back toward 50%)
Penalty kill recovering toward league average

confidence.note: 21 games is a modest sample, but record, goal difference and luck indicators all agree.
